title: THE HIDDEN WEB
thesis: The data of the internet travels through cables lying on the seabed — a network laid over 170 years, still at the mercy of nets, anchors, whales, and the rivalries of nations.

evidence.claim: Submarine cables carry 99 percent of the data traffic that crosses the world's oceans.
A submarine cable moves data in the terabits per second, while a satellite typically offers about one gigabit per second: a ratio of more than 1000 to 1.
Satellites handle less than five percent of global data transmission, a share some estimates put as low as 0.5 percent.
Modern undersea cables are typically about 25 millimetres in diameter and weigh around 1.4 tonnes per kilometre in their deep-sea sections.
Most cable routes run through deep water, where the seabed grants a measure of protection from fishing and storms.
Antarctica is the only continent still without a submarine cable link, so its bases rely on satellite relays with limited capacity.
An Antarctic fiber cable would have to survive minus 80 degrees Celsius and ice sheets moving up to 10 metres every year.
Melting Arctic ice has opened routes for projects like Polar Express, spanning 12,650 kilometres, and Far North Fiber, spanning 14,500.
The internet relies on a web of cables whose exact positions are public knowledge.
In 1842 Samuel Morse submerged a wire insulated with tarred hemp and India rubber in New York Harbor and telegraphed through it.
The first transatlantic telegraph cable became operational on 16 August 1858, linking two continents for the first time in an instant.
That first 1858 cable worked for only about a month before the technology of the day failed it.
Attempts in 1865 and 1866 aboard the world's largest steamship, the SS Great Eastern, produced the first successful transatlantic cable.
By 1872 every continent except Antarctica had been linked by submarine telecommunications cables.
In 1896 the world had 30 cable-laying ships, and 24 of them were British.
British companies owned two-thirds of the world's cables in 1892, and by 1923 their share was still 42.7 percent.
Britain's first act after declaring war on Germany in 1914 was to cut the five cables linking Germany with France, Spain and the Azores.
The first trans-Pacific telegraph cables were completed in 1902 and 1903, linking the United States to Hawaii, Guam and the Philippines.
Early telegraph cables wrapped a copper core in gutta-percha, a natural polymer with almost ideal insulating properties.
TAT-1, the first transatlantic telephone cable, was inaugurated on 25 September 1956 carrying 36 telephone channels.
Early telephone repeaters were powered by high-voltage direct current sent down the cable's inner conductor.
The first-generation cable repeaters remain among the most reliable vacuum tube amplifiers ever designed.
Many 1960s coaxial cables are still usable but were abandoned because their capacity is too small to be commercially viable.
TAT-8, the first fiber-optic transatlantic cable, went into operation in 1988 with two working fiber pairs and one backup.
In 1942 submarine cable technology was adapted to create the world's first submarine oil pipeline, Operation Pluto.
Cable capacity grew so large that satellites could no longer back it up, forcing nets to reroute around the seabed instead.
Modern optical repeaters use erbium-doped fiber amplifiers, first installed in submarine cables in 1995.
Cable repeaters are powered by a constant direct current of 3,000 to 15,000 volts, feeding up to 16.5 kilowatts into the line.
The optical fiber in undersea cables is so clear that runs of more than 100 kilometres between repeaters are possible.
Unrepeated cables as long as 380 kilometres were in service by 2014, carrying their own pump light to remote amplifiers.
Wavelength-division multiplexing lets one fiber carry many laser channels at once, capped by the spacing and bandwidth of amplifiers.
Spatial-division multiplexing cables run at least 12 fiber pairs, and cables with up to 24 pairs have been deployed.
A 2012 trial carried error-free 100 gigabit-per-second signals across 6,000 kilometres of Atlantic route, and one cable can move tens of terabits per second.
Fastest transatlantic round-trip latency is under 60 milliseconds, close to the speed-of-light floor for an all-sea route.
A typical multi-terabit, transoceanic cable system costs several hundred million dollars to construct.
A speculative rush poured more than 22 billion dollars into privately financed cables between 1999 and 2001, ending in bankruptcies like Global Crossing.
Between 1998 and 2003 roughly 70 percent of undersea fiber-optic cable was laid in the Pacific.
In July 2009 a cable owned in part by African investors plugged East Africa into the wider internet, delayed a month by coastal piracy.
Between 1959 and 1996, fewer than 9 percent of cable breaks in the Atlantic and Caribbean were caused by natural events.
Cable faults averaged 3.7 per 1,000 kilometres each year from 1959 to 1979, dropping to 0.44 per 1,000 kilometres after 1985.
Widespread burial of cable beginning in 1980 cut the fault rate to a fraction of its earlier level.
Cable breaks remain routine, with more than 50 repairs a year in the Atlantic Ocean alone and serious failures in 2006, 2008, 2009 and 2011.
Cables in waters shallower than 2,000 metres are now regularly buried against fishing nets and bottom trawling.
Fishing vessels are the leading cause of accidental damage to submarine communication cables.
In 1873 a whale damaged the Persian Gulf Cable between Karachi and Gwadar, tangling its tail in loops of cable and drowning.
Whale entanglement ruptured cables 16 times between 1877 and 1955, 13 of them involving sperm whales.
In 2013 three divers were arrested for severing the main cable linking Egypt with Europe, drastically cutting the country's internet speed.
The 2022 Tonga volcanic eruption cut the island's only cable, a break declared a national crisis that took weeks to repair.
In February 1959, 12 breaks struck five American trans-Atlantic cables; a US naval vessel detained a Soviet trawler that had shadowed each of them.
Two Baltic Sea cable breaks in November 2024 were called a hybrid action, because no one believed the anchors were accidental.
Russian fishing vessels were reported passing over a damaged submarine cable up to 20 times in 2022.
After the Nord Stream sabotage, NATO increased patrols and monitoring of undersea infrastructure.
China's Digital Silk Road funds cable projects through firms like HMN Technologies, which holds up to 10 percent of the global market.
Chinese involvement in roughly a quarter of global submarine cables could let its networks reroute data and apply political pressure.
Submarine cables are governed by UNCLOS articles that protect laying and repair, yet key states such as the United States and Turkey have not ratified the treaty.
During the Cold War the US Navy and NSA tapped Soviet undersea lines in Operation Ivy Bells.
Shore stations can now locate a cable break with spread-spectrum reflectometry, gathering a complete data set in 20 milliseconds.
